articles.title: Chain of custody
articles.content: LAST month, at the London School of Economics’ Environment Week, the International Growth Centre asked a roundtable of policymakers, researchers and funders how evidence systems should change to support harder climate choices. I opened with a case: a major climate decision Pakistan took without the evidence it needed. The obvious case is the 2022 floods. The obvious diagnosis is that the evidence did not exist. The case is obviously right. The diagnosis is obviously wrong. When a third of the country went under water, every decision that followed, from evacuation to the Geneva appeal, was taken in the dark. Yet the Met department had forecast an above-normal monsoon. The national socio-economic registry held geo-coded records on 38 million households. River and satellite data sat with Wapda, the Federal Flood Commission and Suparco. The knowledge existed, in different buildings. No one was mandated to bring it to the table. Pakistan does not have a data shortage. The usual verdict is poor coordination. That is the wrong word. Coordination is voluntary. What Pakistan lacks is a chain of custody: someone legally obliged to carry evidence to the point of decision. The five federal agencies that hold hazard data share no protocol. The roundtable framed three tensions: whether evidence serves the decisions governments actually take, whether it arrives in time to be used, and whether it supports implementation or only design. In Pakistan, each tension marks a break in that chain. Each break has a price tag. Evidence and decision: Pakistan’s research agenda follows what funders find easy to finance, not what the state must prioritise. A warning system has four parts: knowing the risk, forecasting it, getting the message out, and making people act on it. Since before the 2022 floods, the money has gone to the first two. Radars can be procured, counted and inaugurated. Dissemination and response are institutional work. They are not as lucrative as procurement tenders. Nor has the state compiled basic baselines: tested district plans, embankment condition, maintenance costs. That absence is political economy. The reason is elite capture: new schemes bring contracts, win constituencies and visibility. Maintenance brings none. Speed and usability: Pakistan models slowly what it needs fast and leaves its fastest evidence unconnected. The five federal agencies that hold hazard data share no protocol. In Buner in August 2025, a red alert was in force and households still did not move. No one told them what to do, and local governments had no assigned role in last-mile delivery. An SMS that says a flood is coming is information, not a warning for immediate action. The BISP registry is a simpler case. Laid over hazard maps, it could tell a provincial authority within hours who stands in the path of a surge and how to pay them. It is the most decision-ready evidence Pakistan owns. It costs nothing new to produce. Usable evidence in Pakistan rarely needs a better model. It needs a legal duty to share and an interface between databases that already exist. Implementation and capability: This is where costs are highest and evidence thinnest. After 2022, cash transfers were the state’s fastest instrument. They reached only households already on the registry. Exclusion ran to a third in some districts, and nearly half the unregistered did not know how to register. The design was sound. No one was tasked with the evidence that would have exposed the gap during delivery. Damage assessment has no owner either. No platform links damage to recovery, and there is no loss and damage registry. The 2022 needs assessment was built for the Geneva appeal, not the reconstruction. Pakistan chaired the G77 when the loss and damage fund was agreed at COP27. A country that cannot document its losses will struggle to draw on the fund it fought to create. After the 18th Amendment, disaster management and irrigation are provincial; hydromet data, the registry and international finance are federal. Evidence must cross that line twice: up for financing, down for delivery. When a donor project closes, its capability leaves with it, because the analysts sat in a project unit, not a line department with a budget head. The cost of moving blind: These are not administrative inefficiencies. They are why Pakistan’s development agenda is now set by its flood cycle rather than its plans. The 2010, 2022 and 2025 floods each erased growth, reopened IMF negotiations and diverted development money into rehabilitation and reconstruction. Every rupee spent rebuilding what better evidence could have protected is a rupee taken from schools, clinics and the investment that would shrink the next shock. The logic is simple: the Global Commission on Adaptation estimates that 24 hours’ warning of a coming storm can cut the damage by 30pc. High-tech or grassroots: My notes for the roundtable ended with a question for funders: should a country like Pakistan invest in predictive modelling or in grassroots readiness? It is a false choice. The answer is sequence. Better models will lengthen lead times and should be pursued. But a 72-hour forecast is worthless to a household off the registry, in a town with no local government, receiving a non-specific message. The next rupee should buy a messenger, not a model. Moving forward: Three steps, in sequence. First, assign ownership. Notify a binding data-sharing protocol across federal and provincial agencies, and name one owner for assessment data. Informal sharing must become a legal duty. Second, connect what exists before the next monsoon. Link the registry to hazard maps in every province. Compile the missing baselines and open a loss and damage registry. Give local governments a formal role in warnings. Third, commission evidence to decisions. Funders, including those around that table in London, should finance all four parts of the warning chain, not the two that are easiest to procure, and embed analysts in provincial departments under budget heads that outlive the project. Pakistan does not lack evidence. It lacks a chain of custody. Until someone is responsible for carrying knowledge to the point of decision, every flood will end with the same verdict: the data existed, and no one was duty-bound to use it.
articles.author: Ali Tauqeer Sheikh

articles.title: Talking about the exchange rate
articles.content: THERE is an enduring consensus in Pakistan that the exchange rate should not be allowed to move by much as a matter of routine, and that determining its level is a matter of discretion for the state. In some areas we call this “Dar-o-nomics”, after Ishaq Dar, whose name came to be attached to exchange rate policy not because he invented it, but because he has been its most important and visible advocate. Otherwise this thinking dates back to Ghulam Ishaq Khan, who was of the mind that the state should liberalise the economy in such a way that it does not lose its commanding position as the arbiter of all economic outcomes. From deciding the exchange rate, to deciding who gets to make how much profit and what should be the normal indexed rate of return on private capital in the economy, GIK wanted a model of liberalisation that kept all these decisions firmly in the hands of the government. Nowhere is this thinking more clearly stated, and perhaps to more devastating effect, than around how it treats the question of the exchange rate. Over the years many have given voice to this thinking in different ways, and their arguments cluster around three basic assertions. One, devaluations lead to a hike in the rupee-denominated debt service burden. Two, devaluations do nothing to boost exports, they only provide a short-lived impetus that is quickly frittered away as costs of imported inputs rise accordingly, and exporters are forced to pass the price benefit on to their buyers. Three, devaluation causes inflation that burdens the poor disproportionately. None of these assertions is wrong. What is wrong, however, is deploying them in defence of a fixed exchange rate. What all those who have used these assertions over the years have failed to do is actually study Pakistan’s own episodes of exchange rate devaluation. Were they to do that, they would realise that devaluations in our own history have nothing to do with restoring export competitiveness or anything quite so grand. In truth, devaluations are forced upon us because the supply of dollars relative to the supply of rupees in the economy shrinks to a point where a mass stampede breaks out with everyone rushing for the exits. Devaluations have to be undertaken to reflect the new reality of supply and demand of FX liquidity, and to halt the stampede. That’s all. To all those who want to talk about the exchange rate, I ask them to study three episodes from Pakistan’s own history when devaluations happened. The first was in 2007 and ran till late 2008. The second began in late 2017 and ran till 2019. The third episode began in the middle of 2021 and ran till the middle of 2023. These three cycles teach us everything we need to know about exchange rate management. Devaluations in our own history have nothing to do with restoring export competitiveness or anything quite so grand. Each episode happened when Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves were depleting fast in the face of skyrocketing import and debt service bills. In each episode the government chose to first hold the ground and finance the outflows using borrowed money. In each episode they hit a point where further financing was insufficient to meet the pace of the reserve erosion. And in each episode the government hit a point where they had no choice but to reprice the dollar to reflect the new reality of its supply versus demand. In short, in each episode the government chose to drive blindly towards a cliff. So the question to ask is what they were telling themselves along the way. The pattern is the same every time. Reserves peak, the government of the day boasts about having built “record high reserves”, and then the trade deficit begins to swell. For a few months remittances cover the trade deficit so there is no urgency to act. Then the current account swings into deficit and remains there, and then the deficits begin to grow. The government borrows to replenish the reserves. The borrowing hits a limit, the current account deficit marches along, and reserve depletion accelerates. What are they telling themselves during these times, when the pressure is mounting but has not yet reached catastrophic proportions? It has been my unpleasant duty to have covered all three of these cycles over the past two decades, and I can confirm that in each episode they tell themselves the same thing. First, that the current account deficits are temporary, or driven by one-off factors. When the reserve erosion begins to trigger a flight into the dollars, they argue that administrative measures are required to stem the outflows and bring stability back. When they are advised to reprice the dollar before things get out of hand, they respond that exchange rate adjustments do nothing to increase exports, while they produce harm for the country in the form of higher debt service bills and inflation. Eventually they all succumb. They succumb for the simple reason that you cannot endlessly spend money that is not yours to spend. And when they succumb, they grumble and complain. But they never derive any lessons from what they have just lived through, and what they have just seen happen in front of their eyes. What is it they say about those who fail to learn from their own history? They are doomed to repeat it. This is why we have been through this cycle three times already. And yet, today, one more time, we can see people in positions of power, once again, start to repeat the same old nonsense all over again. Once again people who have no idea of what Pakistan’s experience with the exchange rate has been are trying to build arguments on how to manage it. And once again, they are trotting out the same tired old tropes, thus setting the stage for round four of this unhappy roller coaster for yet one more ride. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: LIGO, not Lego
articles.content: WE Pakistanis excel individually, but abroad. We fail collectively, at home. Our role models are either dead or live in self-exile. The best among the best must be our first Nobel Laureate — Dr Abdus Salam. The son of a schoolteacher in Maghiana, a hamlet in Jhang district (Punjab), he won a scholarship to Government College, Lahore, at the precocious age of 14. He studied locally for another two years until he passed his FA exams, with unbeatably high marks. His academic trajectory took him to Cambridge University and then into a higher empyrean when, in 1979, he won the Nobel Prize in physics. He placed its gold medal around the neck of his former teacher Anilendra Ganguly, the man who had inspired him to study mathematics. Dr Salam died in 1996, disillusioned and disappointed, a modern Socrates poisoned by the prejudice of his compatriots. Other Pakistanis who have excelled are Dr Azra Raza, the famous Karachi-born oncologist who has made impressive strides in cancer research; Dr Salima Ikram, a leading Pakistan-born Egyptologist; and Dr Nergis Mavalvala, the renowned astrophysicist and currently dean, MIT’s School of Science. Great minds testify to the capacity of the human brain. Dr Azra Raza has done for cancer research and Urdu poetry what Marie Curie did for radium and radioactivity. To hear Dr Raza speak on her work, which she does but not often enough in Pakistan, is to learn how cancer can be arrested, often at source. Had Dr Azra been born 5,000 years ago in ancient Egypt, she might have made the pharaohs concentrate more on preserving life rather than preparing vainly for an afterlife. Dr Salima Ikram’s studies in Egyptology deepen the digs into a civilisation that paralleled our own Indus Valley civilisation — but without the unguents, the rituals and the gilded funerary objects. If 5,000 years into the past is a long time, Dr Nergis Mavalvala’s work takes us billions of light years away, into galaxies beyond ours. She was inspired by Einstein’s 1915 general theory of relativity, which described “space and time as something that can stretch and compress, rather than a fixed stage”. Einstein believed that “a violent enough event should send a disturbance rippling outward through space and time themselves”. He left it to future generations to measure those ripples, known as gravitational waves. Dr Nergis, her mentor Dr Rainer Weiss (who won the Nobel Prize for physics in 2017) and their team pioneered the study of gravitational waves through the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) project. On Sept 14, 2015, LIGO scientists detected a signal that emanated from the collision and merger of two black holes, each about 30 times the mass of our sun. The signal came from 1.3 billion light years away. It lasted only a fraction of a second but was recordable. Suddenly, man no longer needed a telescope to see the universe through light waves. These can suffer distortion. Purer gravitational waves captured on ultra-sophisticated equipment could be heard. Subsequent improvements in LIGO’s instruments enabled scientists to announce last year that, after detecting over 300 such black hole mergers, they could confirm Einstein’s predictions and Dr Stephen Hawking’s theorem regarding black holes. Dr Nergis, like all great minds, has the ability to compress complicated concepts into assimilable ideas. Many of her brilliantly simplified presentations are available at the click of a button on YouTube. Audiences in Karachi and Lahore were privileged to hear her in person recently. She spoke to them from an intellectual height, which is where their heads should have been. Minds like hers which can comprehend infinite galaxies, billions of light years, millennia of history, or, like Mao Zedong, foresee centuries into the future, testify to the limitless capacity of the human brain. Edgar Snow, in his Red Star over China, recalls Mao and his wife watching a moth give its life to a candle. Charmed by its wings, “shaded a delicate apple-green fringed in a soft rainbow of saffron and rose”, Mao presses the lifeless gossamer of colour into a book. And, after the gruelling Long March, Mao composes a poem which ends: And then, the last pass vanquished, Three Armies smiled. Snow asks whether such people can be thinking seriously of war? One is reminded of A.B. Vajpayee’s poem that he recited in Lahore: Hum jang na honay deynge, khoon ka rang na honay deynge. [We will not allow war, nor let its blood colour us.] A human brain weighs 1.4kg, consists primarily (60pc) of fat, and contains 100 billion neurons. Imagine the waste, if the folly of one unthinking mind trumpeting war, pressed a button and annihilated our entire past, all our present, and the limitless possibilities inherent in our future.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Broken people
articles.content: TWO sanitation workers, 17-year-old Vanesh and 35-year-old Ramesh, tragically died while cleaning an underground tank at a building in Bhimpura, Karachi, on Sept 10. These deaths occurred exactly in the same manner and for exactly the same reason as the deaths that occur week after week in the sewage gutters of Pakistan. Cruelly exploited sanitation workers, compelled by poverty, are made to enter raw gutters to clean faecal matter with their bare hands, under barbaric and inhumane conditions. Some never come out alive. Those who make it back to the surface emerge with bruises, cuts and wounds with the filth having permeated not just their bodies, but their entire existence. More than two dozen sanitation workers have died in sewage gutters across Pakistan this year. They were unknown privately contracted individuals, not listed as employees of any organisation. No individual or organisation was held accountable for gross criminal negligence. The families of the deceased were silenced by giving a few thousand rupees to sign a certificate that they shall not pursue any legal action. The unconcerned state looked the other way, as if nothing ever happened. There were no investigations, no FIRs, nor any compensation. Those who caused these deaths continued to live a life of luxury and were never held accountable. In a landmark judgment delivered on Aug 13, 2026, the Bombay High Court declared that the families of deceased sanitation workers would be compensated by the state or the government agency, even if the death occurred because of work undertaken by a private contractor. This direction unequivocally places the compensation obligation on government entities and not private employers, thus protecting vulnerable families from running after the reluctant private entities for compensation. The court also determined the compensation value at Rs30 lakhs per deceased worker. How come no one in Pakistan questioned the fact that none of the two dozen sanitation workers who died this year were employees of the government departments who are paid billions to do this job. Should we not ask as to why we have parked highly paid managing directors in dysfunctional organisations such as Karachi or Hyderabad Water and Sewerage Corporations or the Water and Sanitation Agencies of Punjab? Why does no one in Pakistan question the uncomfortable paradox: how come all those who died were non-Muslims? Vulnerable citizens cannot be left to die because of negligence. Globally, the practice of sending workers into sewerage systems for cleaning and desilting has been largely eliminated and replaced by mechanised equipment and modern technologies. Several countries including India have also enacted legal prohibitions against such practices, recognising them as incompatible with human dignity and occupational safety. Pakistan today possesses both the technology and the capacity to adopt safer alternatives. Mechanical sewer-cleaning equipment is now readily available, while major utility organisations already possess fleets of mechanised cleaning vehicles. Pakistan cannot continue to practise cruelty and inhumanity in dealing with its minorities and its most vulnerable citizens. They cannot be left to die because of the negligence, incompetence or criminal failure of individuals and organisations. A state that has achieved distinction in high-speed legislation can easily and urgently pass a bill that states: “No worker shall be required or permitted to enter sewage gutters, manholes, drains, or septic tanks for the purpose of cleaning, desilting, or removing blockages. Such activities shall be carried out through mechanical means and equipment.” Any order, instruction or permission to enter a sewage gutter for cleaning could be declared a cognizable offence, and the head of the organisation made to bear direct legal responsibility. A nation with the slightest conscience, humanity or remorse must begin by legislating the above-mentioned prohibition and ordering a judicial inquiry to investigate all deaths that took place in the last one year. The state must register FIRs against the responsible organisations and individuals, even where a settlement was reached with the families of the deceased. If the families of Gul Plaza victims could be compensated by Rs10 million each, why can the state not exemplify the same generosity for its non-Muslim citizens? The adoption of these measures could demonstrate our nation’s forgotten commitment to human rights, occupational safety, and social justice. Must the healing of our most oppressed, brutalised and broken people not be our first step towards building a progressive Pakistan?
articles.author: Naeem Sadiq

articles.title: Conundrum
articles.content: NEITHER side, it seems, has committed fully yet. Both the government and the opposition have engaged in a lot of political chest-beating since the breakdown of negotiations early Sunday, but they have both also left the door open for resumption of dialogue. It is a prudent strategy. The PTI’s plan seems to be to take its protestcaravanon, for lack of a better phrase, a long march along eastern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before it arrives at the gates of Punjab. Meanwhile, the government may be breathing fire, wagging its fingers at the opposition and declaring the inevitability of emergency rule in KP, but it is also signalling a willingness to return to the negotiating table. The president, for all his party’s huffing and puffing, also seems to have decided that pressing the nuclear button is not the wisest choice available at the moment. He, too, has advised the prime minister to give negotiations another chance. That is precisely what the two sides should do while the marchers are still marching and something can be done to dissuade them from heading to Islamabad. It may be difficult for the two sides to reengage after Sunday. Perhaps it may be best to encourage a small group of negotiators to quietly restart the talks while the political drama plays out in the background. The process should start sooner rather than later, before the stakes become too difficult to manage. Both the government and the opposition will have learnt enough from the first round of talks. They now know better what the other side’s red lines are and should adjust accordingly. The government should realise that the opposition to military operations in KP is a bigger challenge than it frames it as, and the KP government should contribute constructively to the security conversation and not act like a spoiler. It still defies understanding why the government remains so unyielding on allowing any relief for jailed PTI founder Imran Khan. On the one hand, federal ministers accuse the PTI of holding the state hostage, yet on the other, the government insists on holding a widely popular public figure in complete seclusion, in defiance of court orders. Showing some flexibility on this matter, as a political concession if not on humanitarian grounds, would earn the government considerable goodwill, allow the opposition to call off its protest and perhaps even break the deadlock over how KP’s security situation is to be handled. That said, the PTI must also engage in talks with transparency and clarity of intent. There can be no last-minute changes of heart when so much is at stake. The two sides came close to a breakthrough in the last round. It is hoped that they can cross the finish line on their second attempt.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Gaza’s torment
articles.content: THREE years since the Oct 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, the people of Gaza continue to face a nightmarish existence. Israel has tightened its siege of the occupied Strip, while a supposed ceasefire has failed to stop the bloodshed. Moreover, the aftereffects of the event continue to reverberate across the Middle East, as Israel has gone on the rampage against several regional states, with the US joining some of these misadventures. The people of Gaza were living in abject misery before the Hamas attacks; the Palestinian resistance group’s actions — effectively an attempt to break the Israeli siege — only gave Tel Aviv an alibi to attack the occupied territory with greater ferocity. Over 74,000 people have been murdered in Gaza since Oct 2023, the vast majority of them civilians. Even a ceasefire in effect since Oct 2025 has failed to stop the violence, with over 1,400 killings during the ‘truce’. Whole families have been wiped out, and experts say Gaza’s people will live with these scars for generations. Aid group Doctors Without Borders says Israel is “asphyxiating Gaza … and continuing its genocide”. While this is the situation on the ground, the supposed peace process is stalled because Israel refuses to end its occupation, even though Hamas has agreed to hand over its weapons. Meanwhile in the West Bank, radical Jewish settlers have unleashed a reign of terror on the Palestinians. Beyond the occupied Palestinian territories, Israel has grabbed more Lebanese and Syrian land, while attacking Iran and Yemen. The lessons from Oct 7 tell us that when a people are denied their basic human rights, are deprived of their ancestral land, and face obscene violence on a daily basis, they will fight back with any means necessary. Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians living under its occupation was criminal; its reaction to the Oct 7 attacks has been genocidal. Peace in the Middle East will be meaningless unless all occupied Palestinian territory is liberated, and Israel is made to pay for its murder of innocents. The two-state solution remains an unattainable dream thanks to Zionist intransigence, while other fanciful ‘solutions’ trumpeted by the Board of Peace are a cruel joke on the Palestinian people. There will be no peace unless there is justice for Palestine.
articles.author: Editorial
